sentences.text: Janenschia robusta is the sole species within the extinct genus Janenschia, representing a massive, four-legged plant-eater from the Late Jurassic era.
This quadrupedal herbivore grew to an impressive length of 24 meters and stood 6 meters tall, with a femur measuring exactly 1.38 meters in length.
The species name 'robusta' was selected to reflect the animal's notably heavy and sturdy physical construction.
At 24 meters long, this dinosaur represents one of the largest known land animals of its time.
Its specific name highlights a unique trait: an exceptionally robust and heavy body plan compared to other contemporaries.
Remains of this creature were unearthed in the Tendaguru Formation, located in the Lindi Region of present-day Tanzania.
After excavation, the fossil materials were shipped to the Stuttgarter Naturaliensammlung museum in Stuttgart, Germany, for study.
In 1908, Fraas identified two skeletons as separate Gigantosaurus species, designating the partial skeleton SMNS 12144, which contained only a right hind limb, as the holotype for G. robustus.
By 1911, Richard Sternfeld moved the species into the genus Tornieria, renaming it T. robusta.
Later, Haughton placed it in Barosaurus, but Nopcsa rejected this, and Wild eventually clarified its distinct status in 1991.
Historically, the genus was assigned to the family Titanosauridae, marking it as the earliest known member of the Titanosauria group.
However, modern phylogenetic studies now classify Janenschia as a non-titanosauriform macronarian sauropod within the broader Eusauropoda lineage of the Saurischia class.
This animal roamed Africa during the Late Jurassic, specifically between 155 and 145 million years ago, or roughly 152 million years ago in the Kimmeridgian stage.
Its temporal range extends into the Tithonian stage, spanning from 149.2 to 143.1 million years ago.

Scientists currently discuss whether certain fossils once linked to Janenschia actually belong to other genera, such as Tendaguria, defined by two anterior dorsal vertebrae, or Wamweracaudia, represented by a specific tail series.

Janensch once argued that G. megalonyx was a forgotten name and that naming rules could be ignored to prevent taxonomic instability, a view Nopcsa later disputed by finding subsequent references to the name.
